GIS Lecture 4 · Buffer and spatial join

Buffer Lab

Which crashes are curve-related? The lab answers with a 150 ft buffer around every horizontal curve on the state routes of GDOT District 7, a Select By Location and a Spatial Join. Run the same three tools here on 769 synthetic curves and 480 synthetic crashes, then change the distance, the units and the end type, and see how much the answer moves.

Step 1 · Load the data

The exercise needs two layers: the crash points you made with Display XY Data and exported to Collisions.shp, and a layer of the horizontal curves on the state routes in District 7. On this page both layers are synthetic: the crashes are invented, and the curves were detected by a program from the bends in the state-route centerlines. State routes and county outlines are context.

Buffer works in the coordinate system of its input. The curves are stored in State Plane feet, so a distance in feet is measured directly on the layer. The crashes are in latitude and longitude; ArcGIS Pro projects them on the fly when it compares them with the buffer. NAD 1983 and WGS 1984 differ by about a metre here, which is small next to 150 ft.

What you are seeing

Try this in class

  1. Leave the buffer at 150 ft, Round, and click through Steps 1 to 4. Write down how many crashes are selected and how many of them are on the same route as the curve.
  2. In Step 2, change the Linear Unit to Meters without touching the 150. How many crashes are selected now? Then choose Decimal Degrees and read the warning.
  3. Press Cluster on the map and flip End Type between Round and Flat. Which crashes drop out, and where are they relative to the ends of the curves?
  4. Drag across the chart from 25 ft to 1,000 ft. Where does the gap between all crashes and same-route crashes open up? Click a few of the crashes in the gap on the map and read their road names.
  5. In Step 4, find a shaded row. Compare Join one to one with Intersect, then Closest, then Join one to many. Which curve's radius does that crash get each time?
  6. Set Dissolve Type to Dissolve all and open Step 4. Why are the curve fields empty, and why did the Step 3 count not change?

How this page decides

Inside a buffer
A crash is inside a round-ended buffer when its straight-line distance to the curve's polyline, in State Plane feet, is no more than the buffer distance. That is the same test as asking whether ArcGIS Pro's round-ended buffer polygon contains the crash.
Flat ends
A flat-ended buffer is cut square at the curve's first and last vertex (its PC and PT). The joints in between stay round, as they do in ArcGIS Pro.
Same route
The crash's Inventory_ route ID and the curve's g_rcd agree in their first 10 characters: county, route type, route number and suffix. The last letter (I or D, the side of a divided road) is ignored. GDOT route IDs are county-based, so a road that crosses a county line changes its ID there; a crash coded to the Fulton piece of a road is not matched to a curve on its DeKalb piece.
First and closest
For a one-to-one join this page takes the first match as the lowest ObjectID among the buffers that contain the crash, which is what ArcGIS Pro's First merge rule gives in practice. Closest uses the curves themselves and their exact distance.

Back to Lecture 4: spatial selection, spatial join, buffer

Slides 7 to 11 and exercise 2 of the 2024 lab (slides 16 to 19) run these steps in ArcGIS Pro. This page runs them on synthetic data.

BufferSlide 7

Create a buffer on the curves to find curve-related crashes. A buffer is a polygon that holds everything within a set distance of a feature.

ArcGIS Pro: Analysis › Tools › Buffer. The tool makes new polygons; it does not select anything by itself.

150 ft, roundSlides 8–9 · lab slides 16–17

The exercise asks for a 150 ft round buffer on the curve layer. Round ends keep a half circle past each end of the curve.

Check: the curve layer is in State Plane feet, so 150 US Survey Feet is 150 ft on the ground.

Select By LocationSlide 10 · lab slide 18

Select the crashes that intersect the buffer. Slide 3 uses the same tool to select the collisions in Fulton County.

ArcMap's dialog called this relationship “intersect the source layer feature”; ArcGIS Pro calls it Intersect.

Spatial JoinSlide 11 · lab slide 19

Join the curve attributes to each selected crash. In the six cases on slide 6 this is the simple join: which buffer is each crash inside, or which curve is closest to it and how far.

Spatial Join writes a new feature class with Join_Count, TARGET_FID and the curve fields, so the stored crash table never changes.

Pitfalls students hit

    A buffer decides by distance alone. Crashes carry a GDOT route ID and milepoint too, so the Linear Referencing Lab asks the same question a second way: same route, and a milepoint between the curve's start and end. Comparing the two answers is a good habit for any safety study.

    Data: 480 synthetic crashes (invented by a program for teaching, all dated 12 April 2023; no real crash record is behind any row), 769 synthetic curves (detected by a program from the bends in the state-route centerlines and shifted up to 10 ft sideways), GDOT state-route segments (GeorgiaRoadSegments_SR.shp, simplified to 15 ft for drawing) and the lab's GA_Counties.shp (FEMA National Risk Index). The map and every distance use a spherical Transverse Mercator in US survey feet on the State Plane Georgia West central meridian (84°10′W) with scale 1 there; the real zone uses 0.9999, so these feet differ from true State Plane feet by up to 1 part in 10,000. Buffers are drawn by stroking each curve with a line twice the distance wide (round joins; round or square-cut caps). Overlap and part counts for dissolved buffers use round-end geometry. “First” stands for ArcGIS Pro's First merge rule, taken as the lowest ObjectID.
